Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Vignette:
Kofi's eyes scan the crowded newsroom, his gaze darting from one face to another, before finally coming to rest on the computer screen in front of him. As a journalist, he is no stranger to chaos, but it's been two years since that fateful night when everything changed. He was covering a protest rally when police opened fire, and Kofi found himself caught in the crossfire. The sound of gunfire still echoes in his mind, making it difficult for him to concentrate on even the simplest tasks. Lately, he has developed a habit of wearing loose-fitting clothing, hoping to blend into the background and avoid drawing attention to himself. His girlfriend, Nia, has noticed the change and asked if everything is okay, but Kofi just shrugs it off, not wanting to burden her with his fears. He has become increasingly withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings and events that might remind him of the friends he lost that night. Certain songs, like the one playing in his car when the police closed in, now fill him with dread. Footsteps behind him make Kofi's heart skip a beat. He quickly turns around, expecting to see someone lurking, but there's never anyone there. His colleagues have grown accustomed to his nervous behavior, but it's starting to take a toll on his work. Editors are breathing down his neck, demanding he meet deadlines, and Kofi is struggling to deliver. He can't shake off the feeling that he's being watched, constantly checking over his shoulder as he walks through the newsroom or heads out for a coffee break. When Nia asks him about his day, Kofi finds it hard to articulate what happened. The memories of that night are still vivid in his mind – more real than any ordinary memory. He can recall the smell of smoke and sweat, the sound of screams and sirens, but when he tries to put it into words, he gets tongue-tied. Sometimes, when he's alone, he hears snippets of conversation from that night, or the wail of police sirens in his head. Kofi used to love exploring new places, but now he avoids unfamiliar neighborhoods, sticking to well-known routes and routines. He can't explain why, but he feels safer this way. Nia has started to notice changes in him, too – how he no longer laughs at jokes or smiles when she walks into the room. Kofi knows what's happening, deep down; he just doesn't know how to stop it. As the anniversary of that fateful night approaches, Kofi feels like he's losing himself. He used to be a happy person, always chasing the next big story, but now he just goes through the motions. He has come to believe that his life was destroyed by what happened – that he'll never be able to do the things that truly defined him as a journalist or a partner. The weight of this realization is crushing him, making it hard for him to get out of bed in the morning. It's Nia who finally convinces Kofi to seek help, pointing out that his avoidance behaviors are no longer working and that he needs professional support to deal with his trauma. As Kofi sits in the therapist's office, recounting the events of that night, he feels a glimmer of hope – maybe it's not too late to reclaim his life, to find happiness again. But for now, he's stuck in this limbo, haunted by memories and crippled by fear.
